item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: An advanced LLM-powered article extraction pipeline delivers a database of buffers for protein studies and protein expression conditions
item.description: Abstract Optimizing protein expression and buffer conditions is a major challenge in life-science research and biotechnology. We present an LLM-powered extraction pipeline that systematically converts unstructured scientific literature into a structured, queryable database. Leveraging advanced optical character recognition, custom reranker models, and large language models, our system achieves ~97% extraction accuracy. By processing 100 353 structural biology publications associated with the RCSB Protein Data Bank, we constructed a database containing 947 153 distinct buffer entries and 73 210 expression protocols for 35 690 unique proteins, establishing the largest resource of its kind. The ProBufEx ( https://www.probufex.org/ ) web platform enables rapid exploration of optimal conditions by protein properties or functions. Case studies reveal distinct patterns in chemical usage on proteins with different post-translational modifications, and function-dependent expression strategies for proteins with different enzymatic activities. This resource transforms vast structural biology literature into actionable knowledge, accelerating evidence-based protocol design, reducing trial-and-error, and streamlining experiments in protein science.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Can autonomous Agentic-AI systems accelerate drug discovery and development in the next decade?
item.description: Abstract The pharmaceutical industry is experiencing a profound transformation driven by rapid advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), increasing research and development complexity, and the expiration of key patents. Agentic-AI systems, which enable autonomous reasoning, decision-making, and adaptive learning beyond traditional data-driven automation, represent a paradigm shift in this context. This review examines the impact of Agentic-AI across the pharmaceutical value chain, including supply chain orchestration, manufacturing optimization, early-stage drug discovery, process development, and regulatory intelligence. These systems enhance operational resilience, reduce development timelines, and accelerate the identification of new therapeutic candidates by fostering dynamic human-AI collaboration. However, the widespread adoption of Agentic-AI introduces significant challenges related to workforce integration, ethical accountability, governance, and regulatory compliance. Addressing these challenges is essential for reliable and scalable deployment. This study identifies key factors shaping Agentic-AI’s influence over the next decade and provides a forward-looking perspective on its evolving role in pharmaceutical innovation.

item.title: Bioinformatics: MR-MAS: an end-to-end multi-agent system for autonomous Mendelian randomization analysis
item.description: Abstract Motivation Understanding disease-related causal mechanisms is essential for biomedical research, yet the practical use of Mendelian Randomization (MR) remains constrained by fragmented analytical workflows and a strong dependence on specialized expertise. These challenges limit the efficient, standardized, and reproducible execution of end-to-end MR analyses. Results We propose MR-MAS, an end-to-end automated MR analysis system built on a multi-agent architecture. MR-MAS leverages the reasoning and coordination capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and integrates external tools to unify data acquisition, causal effect estimation, results interpretation, and manuscript preparation into a single workflow, thereby reducing manual effort. MR-MAS further incorporates a structured Mendelian Randomization Knowledge Base (MRKB) to support MR method implementation and targeted repair of MR analysis code. Across diverse test scenarios, MR-MAS demonstrated stable workflow execution, reproduced several literature-supported causal signals, and maintained consistent causal estimates across repeated runs and different model backends. Additional evaluations showed robust trait retrieval and improved code-repair performance with MRKB guidance. These results suggest that MR-MAS may provide practical support for scalable, standardized, and reproducible MR analyses in biomedical research. Availability and Implementation The source code, MRKB, and benchmark data are freely available at https://github.com/Zaiwen/MR-MAS , with the version used in this study archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20342636 .

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Leveraging mRNA cMH and machine learning for the deconvolution of mixed body fluid stains in East Asian populations
item.description: Abstract Body fluid identification methods have become increasingly well-established, but deconvoluting multi-component mixtures remains a significant challenge. When dealing with complex mixtures, methods based on mRNA coding-region SNPs (cSNPs) still face limitations such as limited polymorphisms of markers and insufficient population specificity. mRNA coding-region microhaplotypes (cMHs), combining tissue specificity with high discrimination power, offer a promising alternative for donor attribution in body fluid stains. In this study, we developed a targeted RNA sequencing panel for East Asian populations, comprising 36 body fluid-specific genes containing 48 cMHs (including 108 cSNPs), along with five genes lacking cMHs. This panel enables both tissue source identification and donor attribution for five types of body fluids and their mixtures. Through specificity evaluation of single-source body fluid stains, we identified six novel body fluid-specific genes. Furthermore, by integrating machine learning algorithms with an in silico mixing strategy, we developed a body fluid classifier that achieved accurate inference for both single-source fluids and complex mixtures. The panel's cumulative discrimination power across the five body fluid types ranged from 0.99568126 (peripheral blood) to 0.99999999 (vaginal secretion). In conclusion, the dual-purpose panel demonstrates robust performance in both tissue source identification and donor attribution for single-source body fluids and complex mixtures.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: WDGTA: a wavelet-denoised graph attention framework for spatial transcriptomics deconvolution
item.description: Abstract Spatial transcriptomics (ST) facilitates the spatial resolution of gene expression profiling; however, many widely used spot-based sequencing platforms capture transcripts from multiple neighboring cells at each location, producing mixed profiles that require accurate cell-type deconvolution. The wavelet-denoised graph attention framework for spatial transcriptomics deconvolution (WDGTA), a graph attention-based framework for ST cell-type deconvolution, was developed and validated on five datasets from two species and four organs. Through the integration of real with pseudo-ST spots, WDGTA introduces a wavelet-based multiscale denoising and reconstruction module, constructs a weighted topological graph using random projection forests, and applies multi-head graph attention to infer cell-type proportions in spatial spots. WDGTA achieved optimal performance in comparison with seven established deconvolution methods. Ablation and discrete wavelet transform (DWT)-specific analyses confirmed the contributions of wavelet denoising, weighted graph construction, and semi-supervised learning. Furthermore, DWT performance remained stable after feature-order perturbation. In mouse brain, cerebellum and ultraviolet radiation (UVR) skin data, WDGTA recovered biologically consistent spatial cell-type patterns and demonstrated robust cross-platform applicability and improved resolution of low-abundance melanocyte signals. Furthermore, it accurately captured melanocyte-associated spatial changes under conditions of UVR exposure and drug intervention. WDGTA provides a unified framework for ST deconvolution across the evaluated tissue contexts. In UVR-exposed skin, it resolved localized melanocyte-associated patterns that were concordant with marker-gene evidence and detected changes associated with UVR exposure and drug treatment. These findings support its use for characterizing spatial cell-type organization and low-abundance cell populations in heterogeneous tissues.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Dynamic perturbation analysis: a modular rewiring framework for decoding cancer stage progression and identifying therapeutic vulnerabilities
item.description: Abstract Disease progression is driven not only by transcriptional alterations but also by dynamic reorganization of molecular interaction networks. However, most existing approaches focus on differential gene expression and fail to capture modular-level reorganization. Here, we present dynamic perturbation analysis (DPA), a modular rewiring framework that quantifies dynamic perturbations across disease stages using a novel metric termed the degree of perturbation. Using gastric cancer (GC) progression as a model system, DPA revealed that extensive modular rewiring persists despite limited stage-specific transcriptional changes after tumor initiation. DPA identified progression-associated perturbation programs characterized by extracellular matrix remodeling, oncogenic signaling activation, stemness acquisition, and late-stage microenvironmental adaptation. Perturbation analysis revealed two major disease-driving programs and prioritized previously unrecognized regulators, including protein tyrosine phosphatase non-receptor type 12 (PTPN12) and leucine rich repeat and Ig domain containing 1 (LINGO1), whose functional roles in GC progression were experimentally validated. Furthermore, modular rewiring-guided drug repurposing uncovered PJ-34 as a promising therapeutic candidate targeting late-stage disease-associated perturbations. Collectively, DPA provides a generalizable framework for decoding disease progression through dynamic modular rewiring, enabling the identification of driver programs, candidate regulators, and therapeutic vulnerabilities. This framework offers a scalable strategy for network-guided mechanistic discovery and therapeutic prioritization in complex diseases.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Ribo-seq rRNA reads reveal co-predicted signatures of ribosome heterogeneity and collisions
item.description: Abstract Ribosome heterogeneity is increasingly recognized as a key factor in various biological contexts, including development, cancer, and immune responses. To enable systematic exploration of this diversity, we previously developed a bioinformatics method that utilized rRNA reads from Ribo-seq data, detecting changes in ribosomal protein composition (dripARF) and ribosome collisions (dricARF) between conditions simply and efficiently. The method works by projecting differences in rRNA read abundance onto the 3D-structure of the ribosome, following which we perform enrichment tests on predefined heterogeneity-specific rRNA position sets. In this study, we apply this tool to publicly available Ribo-seq datasets to understand the impact of experimental protocol variations and to identify shared biological signals across studies. Our analyses show that the rRNA regions assigned to our prediction sets are consistently enriched in rRNA reads, supporting the core assumptions of our approach. We further examine how various protocol factors influence rRNA read distribution and implement a single-sample rRNA position set enrichment analysis-based weight to limit false positives. Finally, we highlight consistent ribosomal changes across these studies, including prominent co-predictors such as ribosome collisions, eS25, and uS19.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Metabolomics workbench: data-driven classification and correlation analysis between metabolite classes, biomarkers, and drugs
item.description: Abstract Public repositories now accumulate an unprecedented amount of metabolomics data. Despite the opportunities for large-scale meta-analyses opened by these repositories, the deposited data rarely becomes systematically re-analyzed. We conducted a systematic metadata-based re-analysis of all human blood metabolomics studies in the Metabolomics Workbench performed using Orbitrap or QTOF mass spectrometry, encompassing 44 165 samples. After harmonizing metabolites with PubChem identifiers and embedding them using SMILES representations, we generated a map of 6752 blood metabolites forming 25 structural clusters, and subsequently performed correlation analysis between these clusters, biomarkers, and drugs. Analysis of 337 120 metabolite pairs detected in at least 10 studies showed that structurally related clusters display correlated abundances (ρ up to 0.6). Correlation patterns among established clinical biomarkers revealed candidate metabolic correlates, several with ρ > 0.7. We also developed open-source software enabling similar analyses for any metabolite across the Workbench data explored. Additionally, curating drug-containing datasets enabled meta-analyses for compounds such as acetaminophen, metoprolol, and atenolol, identifying both known and novel metabolic signatures. Besides the biological insights, we have found that Orbitrap and QTOF tend to detect different metabolites, but they give quantitatively coherent results on overlapping compounds. Overall, the present study provides the methodology and software to perform large-scale mining of public metabolomics data enabling its re-analysis to obtain novel biomedical insights.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Systematic benchmarking of multi-ancestry fine-mapping under variant heterogeneity and LD mismatch
item.description: Abstract Increasingly diverse, multi-ancestry genome-wide association studies (GWASs) provide unprecedented opportunities to better understand the genetic architecture of complex traits. In particular, differences in linkage disequilibrium (LD) patterns across populations can be leveraged to improve the resolution and reliability of statistical fine-mapping. However, cross-ancestry effect heterogeneity, population-specific variant support, and LD mismatches pose substantial challenges, motivating a systematic evaluation of multi-ancestry fine-mapping methods to provide practical guidance for analyses across diverse populations. We conducted a comprehensive benchmarking of nine methods, spanning joint probabilistic models that explicitly model cross-ancestry LD and effect sharing, and univariate-based integration approaches that aggregate ancestry-specific results. We evaluated fine-mapping accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency using realistic simulations derived from UK Biobank genotype data, with real-data validation in the All of Us Research Program. Our study revealed that joint modeling approaches achieve improved power and resolution for causal variants shared across populations. In comparison, post-hoc integration is more robust in recovering causal variants present in only a subset of populations by accommodating differences in variant availability. Moreover, methods are generally underpowered in the presence of systematic discrepancies between GWAS summary statistics and external LD reference panels. Motivated by these complementary performance profiles, we propose the multi-ancestry fine-mapping decision strategy, which avoids a priori method selection by adaptively selecting approaches based on locus-level evidence of ancestry-specific variants. Together, our benchmarking and decision strategy offer practical guidance for robust multi-ancestry fine-mapping and highlight the importance of joint modeling that effectively accounts for ancestry-specific variant availability and LD mismatch.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Prediction of bacteria-specific drug metabolism using a cross-attention-based model
item.description: Abstract Drug metabolism by gut microorganisms is bacteria-specific and can have clinically significant consequences, including prodrug activation, drug inactivation, and the generation of toxic metabolites. However, existing computational approaches have primarily focused on community-level predictions or drug-to-microbe effects, without resolving the metabolic contributions of individual bacterial strains or the bidirectional nature of drug–bacteria interactions, despite advances in computational frameworks. Here, we propose a bidirectional cross-attention architecture, multimodal Bi-MHA, that integrates atom-level molecular embeddings and protein-level bacterial embeddings from pretrained models to generate a combined representation for classification. The proposed model was developed using reliability stratification and a $\mathrm{\lambda}$-scaled loss function on the training dataset and achieved consistent performance across three unseen tasks: unseen drug (receiver operating characteristic area under the curve [ROC AUC]: 0.690), unseen bacteria (ROC AUC: 0.920), and unseen interaction (ROC AUC: 0.949), ranking first among all compared models in the rank-sum metric. Beyond prediction, attention-based analysis not only indicated enzymatic reaction sites that were experimentally validated in previous studies but also prioritized candidate bacterial proteins, demonstrating interpretability at both the atom and protein levels. The proposed model also achieved a 15 percentage point improvement in accuracy over the KNN baseline on an external validation dataset of 85 out-of-distribution drug-bacteria pairs. Furthermore, the model was extended to community-level prediction as a proof-of-concept application using a weighted-abundance pipeline on an independent microbiome dataset. These results demonstrate the model’s potential as an interpretable screening tool for drug safety evaluation and personalized medicine. The source code is available at https://github.com/Jaehyeon-O-Ob/Bacteria-Specific_Drug_Metabolism .

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: AI-bioinformatics synergy for precision medicine in brain diseases: integrating radiomics and multi-omics data
item.description: Abstract The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and bioinformatics is reshaping the landscape of precision medicine in brain diseases, particularly in neurological diseases and brain tumors. Despite advances in both fields, the combined application of radiomics and multi-omics fusion remains underutilized, even though integrative frameworks are essential for addressing the complexity and heterogeneity of imaging and molecular data. This review examines how integrative AI-bioinformatics frameworks enable the fusion of radiomics with genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and other omics modalities to more comprehensively model disease complexity. Leveraging deep learning, graph neural networks, and advanced representation learning, these multimodal systems facilitate biomarker discovery, patient stratification, and personalized treatment strategies. We critically evaluate key challenges including data heterogeneity, limited interpretability, and barriers to clinical validation, and highlight emerging solutions aimed at enhancing reproducibility and translational readiness. Case studies in gliomas, Alzheimer’s disease, and multiple sclerosis illustrate the clinical utility of unified imaging-omics architectures. Ultimately, this review positions radiomics and multi-omics integration as a foundational approach for the next generation of precision medicine in brain diseases by bridging the gap between computational innovation and clinical application.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: UcTCRp: a TCRβ-based framework for identifying and profiling MAIT- and iNKT-associated repertoire signals
item.description: Abstract Mucosal-associated invariant T (MAIT) cells and invariant natural killer T (iNKT) cells are conventionally identified using invariant or semi-invariant TCRα chains, antigen-loaded tetramers, or transcriptomic phenotypes. These requirements limit their detection in public and clinical immune-repertoire datasets that contain only TCRβ sequences. Here we present UcTCRp, a TCRβ-only framework for detecting and profiling relative MAIT- and iNKT-associated signals in bulk immune repertoires. We first identified model-informative TCRβ features, including biased V-gene usage and reproducible CDR3β amino acid composition, in collected human and mouse MAIT and iNKT TCRβ sequences. UcTCRp subsequently integrates these features using species-specific transformer-based representation pretrained separately on large human and mouse TCRβ repertoires, followed by independent supervised modeling with curated MAIT, iNKT, and conventional T cell references for each species. The resulting species-specific models generalized robustly across independent human and mouse cohorts. In paired scRNA-seq/scTCR-seq datasets, UcTCRp recovered transcriptome-defined MAIT and iNKT cells and identified additional MAIT-like candidates supported by receptor evidence but missed by expression-only annotation. Bulk calibration against paired single-cell references and synthetic spike-in experiments established operating characteristics for repertoire-level abundance estimation. These results establish unpaired TCRβ repertoires as an actionable substrate for detecting relative unconventional T cell-associated immune signals, enabling archived repertoire resources to be repurposed for systems-level studies of tissue immunity, disease, and therapeutic response.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Virtual cells: progress and challenges from mechanistic modeling to data-driven integration
item.description: Abstract Virtual cells aim to represent cellular states computationally and predict responses to genetic, chemical, environmental, temporal, and spatial conditions. For comparative purposes, this review uses state encoding (E), state transition (T), and observation decoding (D) as a conceptual abstraction spanning explicit mechanistic models, data-driven foundation and perturbation models, multimodal systems, and spatial and multiscale simulation. We examine model boundaries, data foundations, resource disclosure, out-of-distribution evaluation, causal evidence, and experimental validation. Independent benchmarks show that parameter count and training-set size do not automatically yield robust out-of-distribution generalization, while transcriptomic representations alone do not capture the full functional state of a cell. Trustworthy virtual cells will require perturbation-responsive transitions, cross-modal alignment, continuous-time dynamics, mechanistic constraints, calibrated uncertainty, independent experimental validation, and, where appropriate, closed-loop experimental feedback.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Artificial intelligence in spatial transcriptomics: a review of methods, datasets, and directions
item.description: Abstract Spatial transcriptomics (STs) measures gene expression while retaining the location of transcripts or cells within tissue sections. Unlike bulk RNA sequencing, which averages expression across cell populations, and single-cell RNA sequencing, which generally requires tissue dissociation, ST links molecular profiles to tissue architecture. This spatial information supports the analysis of tissue heterogeneity, cellular organization, and potential intercellular interactions. The spatially resolved nature of ST has unlocked diverse applications in fields such as cancer, neuroscience, reproductive biology, and plant biology. In parallel, the development of publicly accessible databases and repositories has facilitated large-scale, multi-cohort comparisons and benchmarking. The rapid expansion and increasing complexity of these datasets have driven the adoption of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques. These computational tools support a range of tasks, including data pre-processing, image segmentation, spatial domain identification, and pattern recognition. Moreover, they are instrumental in integrative multi-omics analyses and predictive modeling. This AI-focused review provides necessary background on ST technologies and databases and evaluates the use of statistical, ML, and DL methods across the analytical workflow, from image and sequencing-data preprocessing to spatial analysis and LLM-assisted interpretation. We compile key resources related to datasets, AI-driven analytical frameworks, and ST data analysis pipelines, and discuss current challenges, limitations, and future directions for AI-based tools in spatial omics.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Assessing the impact of parental linear gene normalization on the performance of statistical models for circular RNA differential expression analysis
item.description: Abstract Background Circular RNAs (circRNAs) have emerged as promising non-invasive cancer biomarkers due to their stability, abundance in body fluids, and regulatory potential. However, circRNA differential expression analysis (DEA) remains challenging, owing to a lack of consensus on important preprocessing strategies such as filtering and normalization. While well-established bulk RNA-sequencing frameworks are commonly applied to circRNA data, newer approaches such as CIRI-DE (part of CIRI3 suite) integrate linear and circular transcript information to improve detection. Despite developments, an assessment of these integrative strategies is lacking, and the critical impact of filtering on DEA model performance has not been comprehensively evaluated. Results In this study, we evaluated the impact of multiple normalization and filtering strategies on circRNA DEA using experimental datasets, including two in-house blood platelet sets and semi-parametric simulated in silico datasets. Our results emphasize the importance of selecting an appropriate filtering threshold, as overly lenient filtering can reduce model performance across datasets. We found edgeR’s filterByExpr() strategy particularly effective in handling zero counts in circRNA data, while also generating the most reliable results across most datasets.Furthermore, by incorporating linear and circular information as described in CIRI-DE, most methods identified a higher number of DE circRNAs compared to circular counts alone. Notably, circRNAs identified by both CIRI-DE and the modified bulk RNA-sequencing pipelines showed substantial overlap. Conclusion Our findings demonstrate that automated filtering combined with linear-aware normalization significantly enhances the sensitivity and reproducibility of circRNA DEA, providing a standardized framework for more reliable biomarker discovery in transcriptomic research.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: DeepU-PRS: nonlinear and uncertainty-aware SNP heritability modeling for annotation-informed polygenic risk scoring
item.description: Abstract Polygenic risk scores (PRSs) are widely used to quantify genetic predisposition to complex traits, and their predictive accuracy can be enhanced by incorporating functional annotations into single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) effect-size estimation. Existing approaches typically assume linear relationships between annotations and SNP effects, neglecting predictive aleatoric variance and potential nonlinear regulatory interactions. To evaluate the gains of nonlinear and uncertainty-aware modeling, we developed DeepU-PRS, a deep ensemble framework that extends the linear BLD-LDAK model with a neural network trained on functional annotations to jointly estimate SNP heritability and its aleatoric uncertainty, which are then integrated into a Bayesian PRS model. Across 28 continuous and 8 disease phenotypes in the UK Biobank, DeepU-PRS improved the mean continuous R 2 by approximately 10% over linear BLD-LDAK, with the largest gains for traits whose association signals were concentrated, whereas the more diffuse disease traits favored BLD-LDAK. These patterns were reproduced in individual-level data from All of Us. Against a panel of established methods (C + T, Lassosum, PRS-CS, LDpred-funct, and SBayesRC), DeepU-PRS was among the strongest single methods on continuous traits, and ensembles combining DeepU-PRS with the linear baseline and SBayesRC further improved accuracy, indicating complementary predictive signal. These findings highlight the value of modeling nonlinear and uncertain regulatory effects to advance PRS prediction.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Mapping the frontiers of genomic disease surveillance research in the ASEAN region: scientometric insights for precision public health and next-generation epidemic intelligence
item.description: Abstract Genomic disease surveillance has become a cornerstone of precision public health, yet the regional research architecture in Southeast Asia remains insufficiently characterized. This study provides a comprehensive scientometric mapping of genomic surveillance research in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) region and identifies patterns relevant to the development of epidemic intelligence systems. A scientometric analysis of 8129 Scopus-indexed publications (2000–25) was conducted using Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny and VOSviewer software. Analyses included publication trends, citation patterns, collaboration networks, institutional productivity, funding sources, keyword co-occurrence, and thematic evolution. The field demonstrates robust annual growth (14.49%) and high international collaboration (43.92%). Thailand, led by Mahidol and Chulalongkorn Universities, emerged as the principal regional knowledge hub in terms of indexed scholarly visibility. Publication influence is concentrated in a limited set of high-impact journals (PLOS One, Emerging Infectious Diseases, Journal of Clinical Microbiology) and internationally connected author networks. Thematic evolution reveals a transition from molecular epidemiology toward whole-genome sequencing (WGS), antimicrobial resistance (AMR), zoonotic surveillance, and One Health intelligence. Growth modeling suggests sustained expansion through the early 2040s. Genomic disease surveillance research in Southeast Asia has grown substantially, with expanding international collaboration and thematic shifts toward WGS, AMR, zoonotic surveillance, and One Health. However, research output remains concentrated in a few countries and institutions, and bibliometric findings do not measure surveillance capacity or policy implementation. Further research integrating laboratory, funding, epidemiological, and policy evidence is needed across ASEAN.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Decoding cellular vulnerabilities for interpretable drug response prediction
item.description: Abstract Accurate prediction of anticancer drug response remains challenging because conventional approaches based on chemical structures and baseline molecular profiles do not directly capture drug-induced perturbations or cellular dependencies. Here, we present vulnerability-guided cascaded attention transformer (VCAT), which integrates Connectivity Map (CMap)/Library of Integrated Network-based Cellular Signatures (LINCS)-derived consensus transcriptional signatures with clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-supervised cellular representations through adaptive encoders and dual stream cascaded attention. Across four data splitting strategies, VCAT outperformed conventional machine learning and published deep learning models, achieving the best performance in 11 of 12 classification split metric comparisons. Ablation analyses showed that CRISPR-derived vulnerability features complement baseline gene expression and that the proposed interaction architecture further improves prediction. VCAT also enhanced continuous IC50 prediction and generalized across Cancer Therapeutics Response Portal (CTRP), Profiling Relative Inhibition Simultaneously in Mixtures (PRISM), patient-derived organoids, and hepatocellular carcinoma cohorts. Attention based prioritization and integrated gradients jointly highlighted biologically relevant genes, while knockdown of cytosolic iron-sulfur assembly component 3 (CIAO3), methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase 2 (MTHFD2), and WD repeat domain 1 (WDR1) increased sorafenib sensitivity in hepatocellular carcinoma cell lines. These findings support integrating drug-induced perturbations with genetic vulnerabilities for accurate, interpretable, and transferable anticancer drug response prediction.

item.title: Nature Methods: MassNet: billion-scale AI-ready mass spectral corpus empowering scalable deep learning in proteomics
item.description: This Article presents MassNet, a large-scale AI-ready corpus of 1.5 billion MS/MS spectra spanning 35 species, paired with a standardized storage format called Mass Spectrometry DDA Tensor (MSDT). Built on this resource, XuanjiNovo is a nonautoregressive transformer for de novo peptide sequencing that substantially outperforms previous methods.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: Cross-tissue graph attention networks for semi-supervised gene expression prediction
item.description: Abstract High-throughput biotechnologies have significantly advanced precision medicine by enabling the exploitation of global gene expression patterns to enhance our understanding of disease etiology, progression, and treatment options. However, the tissue-specific nature of gene expression presents a challenge, particularly for less accessible tissues such as the brain, underscoring the need for computational methods to accurately impute gene expression in these critical but hard-to-reach tissues. While several attempts to impute gene expression in tissue-specific contexts have shown promising results, their reliance on regression analysis faces limitations due to the inability to capture complex, nonlinear relationships in gene expression patterns. In contrast, modern machine learning techniques, particularly graph neural networks, have demonstrated superior performance by efficiently modeling the intricate interactions among genes across different tissues. Therefore, we introduce gene expression imputation with graph attention networks (gemGAT), a novel approach leveraging GATs to enhance gene expression prediction across different tissues. gemGAT distinguishes itself by predicting the expression of all genes simultaneously, utilizing the full spectrum of genomic data to account for gene coexpressions and nonlinear relationships. Validated through extensive experiments with Genotype-Tissue Expression data and a case study from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, gemGAT demonstrates superior performance over existing methods by efficiently capturing nonlinear gene coexpressions. This advancement underscores gemGAT’s potential to significantly contribute to precision medicine, showcasing its utility in advancing our understanding of gene expression in less accessible tissues.

item.title: Briefings in Bioinformatics: DecBin: Bayesian-optimized deep clustering for long-read metagenomic binning
item.description: Abstract Accurate metagenomic binning is essential for reconstructing microbial genomes, thereby facilitating the discovery of novel taxa, the identification of pathogens, and the characterization of antimicrobial resistance genes. Most existing methods are designed for assembled contigs and cannot be directly applied to raw long reads. Although a few dedicated long-read binning methods have emerged, challenges remain in bin-number estimation and representation learning. Here, we propose Deep Embedded Clustering for Long-read Binning (DecBin), an adaptive method for directly binning raw long reads through integrating a variational autoencoder (VAE), Bayesian optimization, and deep embedded clustering within a unified framework. Computational experiments on large-scale simulated and mock-community datasets demonstrate that DecBin outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both long-read binning and metagenome-assembled genome recovery, while also achieving strain-level resolution in a low-complexity natural microbiome. Further analysis shows that the advantage of DecBin is partly attributable to its Davies–Bouldin index-guided Bayesian optimization, which explicitly evaluates candidate cluster numbers using a global cluster-validity criterion, thereby improving bin-number estimation across communities of varying complexity. Meanwhile, joint fine-tuning of the VAE encoder and clustering layer enables clustering feedback to refine the latent space, yielding representations better aligned with genome partitions. These findings highlight the potential of adaptive deep clustering for metagenomic binning directly from raw long reads without prior assembly. The source code of DecBin is freely available at https://github.com/LorMeBioAI/DecBin .

item.title: Bioinformatics: CRISPR-HAWK: haplotype- and variant-aware guide design toolkit for CRISPR-Cas
item.description: Abstract Motivation Current CRISPR guide RNA design tools rely on reference genomes, overlooking how genetic variation impacts editing outcomes. As genome editing advances toward clinical applications, incorporating population diversity becomes essential for ensuring therapeutic efficacy across diverse populations. Results We present CRISPR-HAWK, a framework integrating individual- and population-scale variants and haplotypes into gRNA design. Analyzing therapeutic targets across 79 648 genomes reveals that genetic variants substantially alter guide performance. For the clinically approved sickle cell disease therapeutic guide targeting BCL11A, we identify haplotypes that completely abolish predicted cutting activity. Across seven therapeutic loci, 82.5% of guides contain variants modifying on-target activity. Variants also create novel protospacer adjacent motif sites generating individual-specific guides invisible to reference-based design. These findings demonstrate that variant-aware selection is critical for equitable genome editing. Availability CRISPR-HAWK is available at https://github.com/pinellolab/CRISPR-HAWK and https://github.com/InfOmics/CRISPR-HAWK .
